messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol Ortega is a 66-year-old editor who came to treatment decades after living through armed conflict in her home country in Latin America, at a time when soldiers and irregular fighters were a visible part of ordinary life. She describes one incident as the moment everything in her body learned that danger could appear without warning. She had been making her way home near dusk when men in uniform moved into the street, shouting orders, and one of them turned toward her with his weapon raised. In the same burst of confusion there was an explosion close enough to throw dust and debris into the air and leave her ears ringing. What stayed with her was not only the bang itself but the sight of the uniformed man’s face fixing on her, the conviction that she had been seen and could be singled out. Even now, she says that when she sees a military or police uniform, hears a bang like an explosion, or unexpectedly catches sight of someone who resembles that offender, her body reacts as if she is back in that street and immediate danger is already upon her.

In the years after she came to the United States, Marisol built a stable life and a long career as an editor, working partly from home and partly in a downtown office. She is divorced and lives alone, and for a long time she told herself she had simply become “careful.” Over the past several years, however, she has noticed that nights have become especially hard. Daytime can feel manageable if she keeps busy with manuscripts and deadlines, but after dark she becomes convinced that safety is fragile and probably temporary. If a car backfires outside her apartment, if a television in a neighboring unit carries the sharp crack of gunfire or an explosion, or if she passes a police officer in the lobby after returning late from the office, the sense of threat rises quickly and remains long after the moment has passed. In those periods she cannot take in reassurance from friends or even from her own reasoning; when others tell her she is safe in her building, in her city, in this phase of her life, she feels that they do not understand how suddenly everything can change.

That persistent sense of danger has begun to shape the conditions under which everyday events become loaded. Because Marisol goes to bed expecting that night is when people are most vulnerable, she sleeps lightly and wakes repeatedly to check the locks, listen at the window, and scan the apartment for signs that someone has come in. She keeps her phone close, sometimes with the lights of the hallway on, and lies still trying to identify every sound. In that state, small noises are no longer small. A metal dumpster dropped in the alley lands in her mind as an explosion; heavy boots on the stairs make uniforms feel near even before she has seen anyone; a stranger’s profile under a cap can catch at her as if she might be looking again at the man who once turned toward her in the street. The more alert she becomes at night, the more readily the world offers up these cues.

The same pattern now intrudes into her work life. As an editor, Marisol often stays late to finish line edits before publication, but she has started arranging her schedule so she can leave before dark and avoid the police presence around transit hubs at evening rush hour. On days when she cannot, the sight of officers in uniform at the station leaves her keyed up for hours, and once she gets home she is almost certain she will not sleep. The next night, already braced and watchful, she notices every bang in the building and every figure outside her window, as if her fear itself has sharpened the outlines of the things she dreads. She does not describe elaborate beliefs about the future; what she says, more simply and stubbornly, is that safety is never something she can trust once darkness falls.

She finally sought help after a recent evening when construction materials crashed near her office with a concussive bang just as two uniformed officers were walking past. She made it home, but spent the whole night waking to check the door, sure that reassurance was useless and that her body was right to stay ready. By morning she was exhausted and ashamed that she had missed a deadline for the first time in years. What frightens her most is not only the memories of the war zone, but the feeling that her nights are narrowing and that the ordinary sounds and sights of her present life are becoming harder to live among. What she hopes for, cautiously, is to believe safety when it is there and to sleep through the night without having to prove to herself, over and over, that she has survived until morning.
